Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the most common tumor presentations about the hip, relevant patient history, physical
examination findings, and histologic and imaging findings.
Describe the role of reconstruction after oncologic resection about the hip.
Explain the balance of the extent of surgical management in relation to disease-specific
outcomes.
Review common hip arthroplasty treatment options for patients undergoing oncologic
resection and reconstruction.

Overview
In patients with primary malignant neoplasms, en bloc resection generally is required for
curative management.
Reconstructive techniques focus on replacing large segments of missing bone about the hip
joint.
In most patients with metastatic disease, surgical treatment focuses on functional
improvement and management of present or impending pathologic fractures.
Techniques focus on attaining immediate fixation in compromised bone via intralesional
procedures. Variations of these procedures can be used in patients with locally aggressive
benign tumors.
Oncologic hip reconstruction commonly is performed to manage malignant bone destruction.
Tumor destruction of bone may result from primary malignant bone tumor or be secondary
to metastatic bone disease.
Metastatic disease to the hip is the most common indication for total hip reconstruction and
most commonly affects patients older than 40 years (Resource 1).
Carcinomas are the most common metastatic tumor, and bone metastasis typically is
managed via radiation therapy after or instead of surgical management.
The differential diagnosis for destructive bone lesions in patients older than 40 years includes
metastatic bone disease, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and primary bone tumors (which are
less common).
Occasionally, total hip arthroplasty is indicated for primary or salvage management of locally
aggressive benign bone tumors about the hip (eg, giant cell tumor of bone, chondroblastoma,
aneurysmal bone cyst).
Epidemiology
Malignant primary bone tumors are exceedingly rare and account for less than 0.2% of all
malignancies in the United States.
Of primary bone sarcomas, osteosarcoma is the most common, with an incidence of 5.6 cases
per million children younger than 15 years; most cases occur in patients in their teenage years.
Approximately 1.5 million new cancer diagnoses are made each year, and bone metastasis is
likely to occur in more than 50% of patients with cancer.
Multiple myeloma is considered the most common primary malignant bone tumor (30,000
persons/year) in the United States. This disease is twice as common in African Americans

compared with Caucasians and affects males more commonly than females (Resource 2).
Primary non-Hodgkin lymphoma of bone accounts for 3% to 7% of primary bone tumors.1,2
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The proximal femur/periacetabular region is a common site of primary bone tumors, including
Ewing sarcoma, osteosarcoma, and chondrosarcoma.
In some patients with metastatic tumors and failed healing of a pathologic fracture or massive
bone loss, replacement of the bone may afford the best pain relief and functional
improvement.
Metastatic and primary bone lesions can occur throughout the skeleton.
Metastatic lesions in the peritrochanteric region are at highest risk for fracture.
Myeloma lesions are common in bones that contain hematopoietic marrow, including the
skull, spine, and long bones.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Suspicion of bone tumor should be increased if patients describe progressive pain unrelieved
by rest.
Patients often report that pain initially was related to an injury but does not resolve with
typical modalities (rest, ice, and NSAIDs).
Timing, intensity, duration, and nature of pain are important to discuss.
Night pain and weight-bearing pain should increase suspicion for tumor-related bone pain.
Patient history of cancer should be obtained.
Questions should be asked about other organ systems.
Lungs: shortness of breath, cough, chest pain, hemoptysis
Thyroid: heat or cold intolerance
Prostate: urinary frequency or pain
Skin: new or changing lesions to suggest melanoma
Colorectal: bowel habit changes or bleeding
Physical Examination

Evaluate for swelling or soft-tissue mass, limp, diminished range of motion, sensory and/or
motor deficits, palpable lymph nodes.
Clinical presentation
Common symptoms include bone pain and pathologic fractures.
Multiple myeloma lesions occur throughout the skeleton but are common in bones that
contain hematopoietic marrow, including the skull, spine, and long bones.
Laboratory findings
Recommend obtaining a complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel,
erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein level, and urinalysis.
In patients with multiple myeloma, laboratory findings may reveal normochromic,
normocytic anemia; hypercalcemia; renal insufficiency; amyloidosis; and elevated
erythrocyte sedimentation rate.
Imaging Studies
Radiographic appearance of bone tumors is variable and dependent on pathologic diagnosis.
Correlating patient age with radiographic findings helps to narrow the differential diagnosis.
Patients older than 40 years who have a destructive bone lesion are most likely to have bone
metastasis, myeloma, or lymphoma.3
Metastatic disease may appear blastic (typically prostate), lytic, or mixed lytic/blastic.
Prostate carcinoma: typically sclerotic but 15% are mixed
Breast carcinoma: typically sclerotic but 25% are mixed
Lung carcinoma: typically lytic but 15% are mixed
Carcinoma of the cervix: mixed
Testicular tumors: mixed
Patients with multiple myeloma typically present with multiple punched-out lytic lesions.
Skull lesions and vertebral compression fractures are common.
In older patients (>40 years) who present with a destructive bone lesion, oncologic staging
studies (CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis or positron emission tomography scan plus
laboratory studies) are the first step in evaluation to define the origin and extent of disease.4
Primary bone tumors have unique radiographic imaging characteristics.
Patients with osteosarcoma typically present with a blastic and destructive lesion and a
periosteal reaction (Codman triangle).
Patients with chondrosarcoma present with a lytic or blastic lesion, rings and arcs of
mineralization, and reactive cortical thickening and scalloped cortices.

Patients with Ewing sarcoma present with a large destructive lesion in the metaphysis or
diaphysis with a permeative appearance; a characteristic periosteal reaction sunburst
pattern often is observed.
Bone Scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy often is positive in patients with sarcoma and most patients with metastatic
disease if an osteolytic or osteoblastic response is present; bone scintigraphy usually is
negative in patients with myeloma because minimal osteoblastic response is present.
Positron Emission Tomography–CT
Currently, positron emission tomography–CT is the preferred imaging modality for multiple
myeloma; however, a skeletal survey is helpful in determining fracture risk.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI is critical to evaluate a bone sarcoma to define the tumor extent and margins for
resection.
Osteosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma often are associated with a large soft-tissue mass.
Chondrosarcoma typically is dark on T1-weighted images and bright on T2-weighted images.
MRI rarely is necessary for evaluation of metastatic disease outside of the spine.
Pathology
In patients with myeloma, the lesion consists of sheets of plasma cells with eccentric nuclei;
little intercellular material is present (Figure 1). Nuclear chromatin are arranged in a clock-face
pattern. Abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm with rare mitotic figures are observed. These lesions
are extremely vascular, with an extensive capillary system. Immunohistochemistry stains are
CD38 positive.

Metastatic carcinoma typically maintains the differentiated cellular features of the primary
tumor, with a glandular appearance.
Bone sarcoma appearance also is variable based on type.
Osteosarcoma has lacey osteoid produced by neoplastic mesenchymal cells; subtypes are
classified by predominant extracellular matrix.
Chondrosarcoma typically has a chondroid matrix and hypercellular stroma and grade-
dependent pleomorphism.
Ewing sarcoma has a monotonous, small, round blue cell appearance with prominent nuclei
and may have pseudorosettes. Immunohistochemistry stains are CD99 positive
Management
Nonsurgical Management
The primary role of nonsurgical management in patients with metastatic hip lesions is pain
control in those at low risk for pathologic fracture.

6/16

Mirels criteria is a risk assessment tool to help providers determine if a metastatic lesion to
bone is at increased risk for pathologic fracture and if management may be warranted.5
Depending on the oncologic diagnosis, the standard of care may include radiation therapy
and/or chemotherapy.
Radiation therapy is effective in diminishing pain, and certain tumors are more radiosensitive
than others.
Management of Ewing sarcoma often involves radiation therapy.
Management of most metastatic carcinoma bone lesions should include radiation therapy.
Potential active chemotherapy agents include the following:
Anthracyclines, alkylating agents, immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors,
monoclonal antibodies, corticosteroids, and diphosphonates or receptor activator of nuclear
factor-kappa B ligand inhibitors (to help decrease bone pain, lesion number, and serum
calcium)
Nonsurgical management of periacetabular metastasis is a viable treatment option with a
combination of modern chemotherapy, radiation therapy, and protected–weight bearing.
Interventional radiology techniques (ablation and cementoplasty) may aid in pain control of
modest lytic periacetabular defects.
Surgical Management
Considerations for Metastatic Disease
Resection Goals
In patients with oligometastatic disease and anticipated long survival, resection improves local
control and may affect disease-free survival.
The primary goal of resection of metastatic disease or benign aggressive disease for total hip
arthroplasty is not complete resection of disease but pain relief and functional restoration.
Reconstruction Goals
Reconstruction should address deficits created during resection or from bone loss because of
metastatic disease, specifically metaphyseal bone, and major tendon attachments for hip
stability.
Hemiarthroplasty is associated with a low rate of reported conversion and a lower incidence of
instability and should be considered in patients without substantial preexisting hip arthritis.

During soft-tissue resection about the proximal femur, the gluteus medius can be
compromised. In this scenario, the tensor fascia and gluteus maximus can be sutured to the
reconstruction to become more important hip stabilizers.
Acetabular Reconstruction
Arthroplasty is the preferred treatment option for pathologic proximal femur fractures.
If arthritis and/or acetabular metastatic disease is present, total hip arthroplasty is
recommended.
Preoperative planning based on oncologic diagnosis is critical to the success of total hip
arthroplasty.
For highly vascular tumors (particularly renal cell metastasis), preoperative embolization is
recommended.
The surgical approach should allow for placement of an antiprotrusio cage if necessary
(typically anterolateral, posterolateral, or trochanteric osteotomy approaches are viable
options).
Fixation methods for acetabular reconstruction include the following:
Harrington reconstruction technique for metastatic disease6
Multiple cancellous screws for fixation of a highly porous acetabular component
Highly porous-coated acetabular component with augments
Highly porous-coated acetabular component with an antiprotrusio cage in a cup-cage
technique
Custom triflange acetabular reconstruction
Studies have shown improved acetabular survival after radiation therapy to the pelvis with the
use of a highly porous-coated tantalum revision component7 (Figure 2).

Femoral Reconstruction
Modular endoprosthetic implants are the standard approach for reconstruction of
considerable bone defects.
Less common tools for reconstruction include allograft-prosthetic composite, Girdlestone
resection arthroplasty, and rotationplasty in skeletally immature patients. Allograft-prosthetic
composite allows for enhanced proximal femur soft-tissue attachments if allograft tendons
remain on graft.
In planning proximal femur replacement, most systems require a minimum resection of 7 to 8
cm.

If less than 7 cm of resection is necessary, a revision hip stem may better facilitate
reconstruction. Multiple companies have revision hip stems that facilitate soft-tissue
reattachment.
Measuring the post-resection length of the proximal femur is beneficial in building the trial and
final proximal femur replacement.
An extensile hip exposure is necessary, typically to the mid shaft of the femur.
If possible, a trochanteric slide osteotomy is the preferred technique if the lateral greater
trochanter can be salvaged during proximal femur replacement. This technique prevents
proximal migration of the gluteus medius because of its continuity with the vastus lateralis.
This fragment is then secured to the proximal femur replacement with the use of heavy,
nonabsorbable suture or wire after final implant insertion.
En bloc resection of the proximal femur is performed for extensive metastatic destruction of
the proximal femur or if the proximal femur must be resected for sarcoma.
A cemented stem proximal femur replacement is the preferred fixation option. The femoral
stem should have a collar and be seated flush on good-quality cortical bone to prevent
subsidence.
Cemented proximal femur replacement is associated with good success, with less frequent
loosening than distal femur endoprostheses.8
A tapered fluted modular stem also is a viable treatment option if good-quality isthmus of the
diaphyseal femur remains after resection and if radiotherapy to this area is not necessary.
A series of conical fluted stems, including proximal femur replacements, showed no loosening
or subsidence9 (Figure 3).

Surgical Considerations for Sarcoma
Resection Goals
Wide resection with negative margins is the mainstay of surgical management of sarcoma.
MRI guides the extent of soft-tissue and bone resection to attain a negative soft-tissue margin.
Selection of surgical approach should primarily allow for adequate margins for resection, with
the secondary intention of optimizing reconstruction options.
Reconstruction Goals
Similar to the management of metastatic disease, reconstruction after sarcoma resection
should address deficits created during resection.
Hemiarthroplasty is a consideration because of the low rate of reported conversion and
instability.
Native acetabular preservation also is preferred in children with primary femoral sarcomas if
continued acetabular growth is expected.
Soft-tissue reconstruction about the proximal femur should be performed to optimize hip
stability.
Acetabular Reconstruction
Similar to metastatic disease, preoperative planning based on oncologic diagnosis is critical to
the success of total hip arthroplasty.
If total hip arthroplasty is performed after acetabular resection, reconstructive options include
the following:
Multiple cancellous screws for fixation of highly porous acetabular component
Highly porous acetabular component with augments
Highly porous acetabular component with an antiprotrusio cage in a cup-cage technique
Custom triflange acetabular reconstruction
Femoral Reconstruction
Modular endoprosthetic implants are the standard approach for reconstruction of
considerable bone defects after sarcoma resection.
In skeletally immature patients with an anticipated substantial leg-length discrepancy,
extendible femoral implants may be used but are associated with a high rate of conversion at

5 years postoperatively.
The same principles for proximal femur reconstruction for metastatic disease apply.
Complications
The most common complications after proximal femur replacement include dislocation
because of loss of the robust hip capsule and muscular attachments (abductors, gluteal sling,
iliopsoas tendon, short external rotators, and vastus lateralis) and infection related to
prolonged surgical time, large potential space, and seroma formation.
Instability is decreased (6% or less) via meticulous soft-tissue reconstruction and performing
hemiarthroplasty if possible.8,10
The risk for neurovascular injury is increased because of the close proximity of the iliopsoas
and profunda femoral artery and because of the risk of stretch injury to the femoral and sciatic
nerves. The limb is easily overlengthened without proximal femur muscular attachments.
Outcomes
The rate of conversion from proximal femur replacement hemiarthroplasty to total hip
arthroplasty is 5.8%, with most revision procedures performed in patients in their teenage
years.8
Revision rates from hemiarthroplasty to total hip arthroplasty have been shown to be high in
patients younger than 21 years.11
Marco et al12 evaluated patients with acetabular metastasis treated via the modified
Harrington technique and reported continued pain relief at 6 months postoperatively in 76%
of the patients. In their cohort, 25% of the patients had moderate local progression of disease,
and multiple patients had failed fixation.
Houdek et al13 compared Harrington reconstruction and porous-coated tantalum acetabular
implants for the reconstruction of acetabular metastatic disease. The authors also reported
that Harrington reconstruction was considerably more likely to require revision surgery.
Abdel et al14 evaluated oncologic reconstruction after wide periacetabular resection for
sarcoma. The authors reported that the most common complications included dislocation,
deep vein thrombosis and wound healing; multiple patients underwent revision surgery for
recurrent dislocation.
